c.tagline: The roof of the world's gateway — cold deserts, turquoise lakes, and the road to K2
langs: English (limited, more common with tour operators)

card: Cash is essential — cards are rarely accepted outside a few upscale hotels. Bring enough PKR cash for your whole stay, including trekking and jeep-safari expenses; ATMs in Skardu town can run out of cash or be offline.

taxi.color: no standard livery — mostly private jeeps and sedans
taxi.fare: Roughly $1-3 within town; day jeep hire for Shigar or the cold desert runs $30-60
taxi.fareNote: Fares are negotiated upfront; a 4x4 is essential for Deosai Plateau, Shigar Valley, and Khaplu

emergency.medical: District Headquarters Hospital Skardu; 1122 Rescue where available
emergency.note: Serious altitude or trauma cases are often evacuated to Islamabad; travel insurance with medevac and high-altitude coverage is essential for trekkers

religion: Islam (predominantly Shia and Noorbakhshi, reflecting Baltistan's distinct religious history)
walk: Skardu town's bazaar and fort area are walkable, but the valley's real highlights — Shigar, the cold deserts, Kachura Lakes, and Deosai Plateau — are spread across the region and require a jeep or private car.

safety.safety: Gilgit-Baltistan overall has a strong safety reputation and Skardu is a well-established base for trekkers heading to K2 and the Karakoram; exercise normal precautions and check current travel advisories
safety.crime: Violent crime against tourists is rare; altitude sickness, road conditions, and weather in the high mountains are bigger practical concerns than crime

hood_landmark.Shigar Valley: Shigar Fort (Fong Khar), now a heritage hotel
hood_landmark.Kachura: Upper Kachura Lake and Shangrila Resort (Lower Kachura Lake)

avoid.reason: Areas close to the Line of Control and some side valleys are restricted or permit-only; the town itself needs only standard precautions.
Crime is rare, but vet trekking guides and operators carefully and treat the landslide-prone mountain roads as the real risk.

hood_desc: The commercial and administrative heart of Skardu, with the main bazaar, budget hotels, and trekking/expedition outfitters arranging Baltoro and K2 base camp treks.
The road leading toward Satpara Lake, with a scattering of hotels offering lake views and easy access to the dam and boating.
A fertile side valley about an hour from Skardu, centered on the beautifully restored Shigar Fort and serving as the launch point for K2 and Baltoro Glacier expeditions.
Home to the turquoise Upper and Lower Kachura Lakes, a favorite day-trip and overnight spot with resort-style lodges.
A striking cold desert of sand dunes against a backdrop of snow peaks, one of the highest-altitude deserts in the world.

water.note: Drink bottled, boiled, or filtered water even though sources are glacier-fed.

transit.sys: No formal public transit; shared Suzuki vans run fixed routes within Skardu town
transit.map: No formal transit map; ask your hotel for van routes
transit.note: Most travelers hire a private jeep for Shigar, the cold deserts, Kachura Lakes, and Deosai Plateau

transport.air: Skardu International Airport (KDU) has direct flights from Islamabad, Lahore, and Karachi (about 1 hour from Islamabad, one of the world's most scenic mountain flights, weather-permitting)
transport.train: No rail service anywhere in Gilgit-Baltistan
transport.bus: NATCO and private coaches connect Skardu to Islamabad via the Karakoram Highway and Skardu road (roughly 15-18 hours)
transport.ferry: None — Skardu is a landlocked mountain town with no ferry service
transport.car: Road distance from Islamabad is about 630 km (15-18 hours); most visitors fly in and hire a local jeep for onward valley trips

airport.name: Skardu International Airport
airport.distance: ~10 km (20 min) from Skardu town center
airport.transport: Taxi or hotel pickup; flights are weather-dependent and frequently delayed or cancelled, so build flexibility into your itinerary

net.m: SCOM (Special Communications Organization) has the most reliable coverage in Skardu and Baltistan; other carriers are patchier
net.w: Wifi is available in hotels in Skardu town but slow and unreliable further into the valleys and at trekking lodges
net.gb: ~$3-6 for a prepaid SIM with a few GB
net.fwn: Some social media and VOIP services face intermittent restrictions; a VPN can help but isn't always necessary
net.ap: A local SCOM SIM (best mountain coverage) is recommended, purchased with your passport in Islamabad or Skardu

tip.s: Tipping (baksheesh) is customary for guides, porters, and drivers — 10% or a fixed daily amount is appreciated, especially for trekking crews
tip.r: Rounding up or leaving 10% is welcomed at restaurants, though not obligatory

food.name: Mamtu
food.desc: Steamed Balti dumplings filled with minced beef or mutton, onion, garlic and green chilli, served with a tangy house sauce.

places.name: Mamtu De Skardu
places.note: Cheap-eat specialist named for the dish, known for its signature dipping sauce.

places.name: Food Street Api Xhoq
places.note: Top-rated stall making mamtu and chapshuro the traditional way.

places.name: Dewane Khas
places.note: Widely called the gold standard for authentic Balti cooking in town.

food.name: Chapshuro
food.desc: The Balti meat pie: minced beef or mutton with onion and green chilli sealed in dough and baked until crisp outside, juicy within.

places.name: Food Street Api Xhoq
places.note: Specialises in chapshuro baked to order in the old style.

places.name: Dewane Khas
places.note: Reliable kitchen for the full range of Balti classics.

places.name: Yadgar Chowk bazaar stalls
places.note: Bazaar bakeries turn out chapshuro through the afternoon.

food.name: Apricot dishes
food.desc: Baltistan's signature fruit appears as sweet dried khubani, apricot soup thickened with kernels, jams and nutty apricot-kernel oil poured over bread.

places.name: Shangrila Resort dining
places.note: Lakeside kitchen serving apricot desserts and preserves from the valley.

places.name: Yadgar Chowk bazaar stalls
places.note: Bazaar rows sell sun-dried apricots, kernels and pressed apricot oil.

places.name: Dewane Khas
places.note: Puts local apricot preparations on an otherwise meat-heavy Balti menu.

food.name: Grilled Indus trout
food.desc: River and lake trout rubbed with salt, chilli and lemon then grilled or pan-fried whole; the mountain valley's most prized fish.

places.name: Shangrila Resort dining
places.note: Iconic grilled trout served beside the heart-shaped lake.

places.name: Rafsal Restaurant
places.note: Very highly rated dining room with sweeping valley views.

places.name: Mount Feast Restaurant
places.note: Terrace dining spot known for generous fish and grill plates.

food.name: Prapu and balay
food.desc: Buckwheat noodles and hand-cut pasta tossed in a garlicky walnut or yoghurt sauce, the everyday winter food of Balti households.

places.name: Dewane Khas
places.note: One of the few restaurants cooking home-style Balti grain dishes.

places.name: Local homestays, Skardu and Shigar valleys
places.note: Family kitchens are the classic place to eat prapu and balay.

places.name: Food Street Api Xhoq
places.note: Traditional-style kitchen alongside the meat-pie stalls.

food.name: Marzan and khurba
food.desc: Rich mountain sweets: marzan is a dark walnut-and-buckwheat paste, khurba a butter-soaked bread eaten at celebrations and in deep winter.

places.name: Local homestays, Skardu and Shigar valleys
places.note: Festive sweets made at home and offered to guests.

places.name: Dewane Khas
places.note: Serves traditional Balti sweets rarely found on other menus.

places.name: Yadgar Chowk bazaar stalls
places.note: Bazaar sweet sellers stock walnut pastes and butter breads.

food.name: Namkeen chai (butter tea)
food.desc: Salted tea churned with butter and milk into a warming pink-grey brew, drunk all day against the altitude and cold. No alcohol is served locally.

places.name: Yadgar Chowk bazaar stalls
places.note: Bazaar tea houses pour salt tea from morning until late.

places.name: Local homestays, Skardu and Shigar valleys
places.note: Every household welcome starts with a bowl of butter tea.

places.name: Dewane Khas
places.note: Offers namkeen chai alongside the traditional menu.

food.name: Apricot juice and tumuro tea
food.desc: Thick pressed apricot nectar, and tumuro, a wild mountain-thyme infusion drunk for altitude and digestion; both are alcohol-free.

places.name: Shangrila Resort dining
places.note: Serves fresh apricot juice from valley orchards.

places.name: Mount Feast Restaurant
places.note: Breakfast buffet spot with fresh juices and herbal teas.

places.name: Yadgar Chowk bazaar stalls
places.note: Stalls sell dried tumuro thyme and pressed apricot drinks.

landmarks: Kharpocho Fort (Skardu Fort)
A 16th-century fort perched on a rocky hill above town, commanding majestic views of the Indus River and Skardu Valley.
Shangrila Resort and Lower Kachura Lake
Pakistan's postcard classic, a heart-shaped emerald lake ringed by orchards and red-roofed pagoda cottages beneath barren peaks.
Upper Kachura Lake
A deep, startlingly blue glacial lake hidden above the Indus, quieter than its famous neighbour and ideal for boating and cliffside walks.
Satpara Lake
A shimmering turquoise reservoir south of Skardu that mirrors surrounding peaks and supplies the town, dotted with a tiny central island.
Deosai National Park
The Land of Giants, a 4,000-metre wildflower plateau roamed by Himalayan brown bears, among the highest plains on Earth.
Sheosar Lake
Deosai's jewel, a deep-blue alpine lake at 4,142 metres with Nanga Parbat rising on the horizon across flower-carpeted meadows.
Katpana Desert (Cold Desert)
Surreal white sand dunes at 2,200 metres that dust with snow in winter, one of the world's highest cold deserts.
Manthal Buddha Rock
A giant granite boulder carved with an 8th-century relief of the Buddha and bodhisattvas, testament to Baltistan's Buddhist past.
Shigar Fort (Fong Khar)
A beautifully restored 17th-century raja's palace of wood and stone in Shigar Valley, now a heritage museum-hotel en route to K2 country.
Khaplu Palace
A magnificent 1840 Balti royal residence blending Tibetan, Kashmiri and Ladakhi styles, restored by the Aga Khan Trust, a superb day trip east.

train.note: There is no railway in Gilgit-Baltistan. Pakistan Railways (https://www.pakrail.gov.pk/) reaches no further north than Havelian. Skardu is reached by the long road from Gilgit or up the Indus gorge from Islamabad, or by the flight from Islamabad, which is scenic but often cancelled by weather.

bus.note: No international coaches - the Chinese crossing is via Sost on the Hunza side, and the Indian frontier along the Line of Control is closed. NATCO and private minibuses run from Skardu to Gilgit in about 6-7 hours on a road carved into the Indus gorge, and long-distance coaches reach Islamabad in 20 hours or more. Landslides close the route regularly.

ferry.note: Skardu sits at 2,200 m on the Indus, which is far too fast and shallow here for scheduled navigation, so there are no ferries. Small boats cross to Kachura and Shangrila lakes as excursions.

half.name: Basho Valley
half.blurb: Forested side valley with alpine meadows and a trout-stocked stream, popular for camping and picnics.

full.name: Hushe Valley
full.blurb: Remote mountain valley used as an approach route for Karakoram peaks, with traditional Balti villages.

full.name: Kharmang Valley
full.blurb: Indus-side valley with apricot orchards and stone villages along the road toward Kargil.
